summary: Aims to focus discussion on problems of policy routing in the Internet and ways to solve them. It does not propose standards. Policy routing means choosing paths according to rules set by network owners, and not just by the shortest distance.

eli5.summary: Some roads have rules about who may drive on them. This asks how the Internet can follow such rules when it picks a path.

questions: policy routing problems in the internet
subtitle: Selecting Internet routes based on administrative policies, not just shortest path.

tldr.problem: Internet routing algorithms select paths based on minimizing delay or hop count, but network operators need to enforce policies restricting which users and services can use which paths for business, trust, or cost-recovery reasons.
tldr.mechanism: Packets carry an abstract policy route (a sequence of administrative regions) that policy gateways verify against local policy terms. Each gateway validates the route and selects the next gateway. End points synthesize routes by matching policy terms across regions, allowing policies to be enforced locally while being coordinated globally.
tldr.outcome: Networks can charge for service based on usage, restrict traffic by user or service class, and enforce bilateral agreements between autonomous regions without requiring global routing computation or topological constraints.

today: RFC 1102 remains experimental and was not adopted as a standard. The proposal anticipated many concepts used in later Internet policy frameworks, such as BGP communities, routing policy language, and quality-of-service routing. However, the full mechanism proposed here was never implemented. Modern Internet routing uses protocol-based policy (BGP route filters, QoS marking) rather than explicit policy routes in packets. The ideas influenced thinking about policy expression and multi-dimensional routing constraints. Some deployment patterns and policy servers echo concepts in this RFC, though without the explicit policy route option in packets.

sections.title: Why Policy Matters in Routing
sections.content: Today's routing protocols select paths to minimize cost metrics like delay, but network operators need to enforce policies that restrict traffic for business reasons: charging for service, protecting networks from unauthorized use, or maintaining bilateral agreements between regions. The Internet is divided into Administrative Regions (ARs), each with its own policies. Existing routing protocols, particularly EGP, imposed topological constraints that do not match real policy concerns. This RFC proposes policy routing where packets carry an explicit policy route, policy gateways verify it against local policies, and end points synthesize routes by matching policies across regions. This allows policies to be set independently by each region while being enforced coordinately.
sections.eli5: Different networks have different rules about who can use them. The routers need to understand those rules and enforce them, not just pick the fastest path.

sections.title: What Policy Routes Are
sections.content: A policy route is an abstract sequence of administrative regions that a packet should traverse, specified by the source end point rather than by intermediate routers. This is a form of source routing, but at the level of administrative regions rather than individual gateways. Each policy gateway (at the boundary between regions) converts the abstract sequence to concrete gateway hops. The advantage is that end points specify legitimate policy concerns (which regions to use) while gateways handle operational details (which specific gateway to use, whether it is up, redundancy). An abstract policy route must be concrete enough to be meaningful but abstract enough to not require end points to know the exact topology of each region.
sections.eli5: Instead of letting each router decide the path, the computer sending the message says which networks it wants to go through. Each border router then picks the exact path within those networks.

sections.title: Verifying Policy Routes
sections.content: As a packet enters an administrative region, the policy gateway must decide whether to forward it based on local policies. The gateway identifies the user via source and destination addresses and an optional User Class Identifier (UCI). It verifies the policy route by checking source and destination regions and the adjacent entry and exit regions against stored policy terms. A policy term is a template that specifies which combinations of source, destination, and adjacent regions are permitted, along with conditions like time-of-day or service type. Conditions must be understood in advance by end points so they can construct compliant routes. The gateway verifies only stable conditions; highly dynamic conditions like queue length should be handled by internal AR engineering rather than policy routing.
sections.eli5: When a message arrives, the router checks: Is this user allowed to use this path? Does the source and destination match what we allow? Are any special conditions met, like time of day or service type?

sections.title: Expressing and Combining Policies
sections.content: A policy term specifies the source and destination ARs, the entry and exit ARs (the adjacent regions), and conditions that must be true. For example, a transit network might write a policy term allowing any traffic from universities to other universities. Another region might allow its hosts to reach any other region via one specific exit gateway. Adjacent regions must have compatible terms for a route to be valid. The RFC shows how to combine terms from multiple regions to form a complete policy route: a sequence of matching terms forms a path from source to destination, like dominoes lining up. More complex policies can be expressed by refining terms based on user identity, host addresses, or conditions. The notation is similar to access control lists, using wildcards and symbols to balance expressiveness with compactness.
sections.eli5: Each network writes rules about what traffic it accepts. Adjacent networks must agree their rules work together. To send a message, you find a sequence of rules that form a path from start to finish.

sections.title: Creating Policy Routes
sections.content: Creating a policy route is a two-step process: synthesis (finding all valid routes) and selection (picking the best one). To synthesize, an algorithm finds matching policy terms in each region, like a path-finding search where each term represents an edge. Each term must be compatible with adjacent terms in billing conditions and other parameters. The result is a list of possible routes, each with associated conditions. Selection is not fully automatic; human judgment is needed because different ARs may use different billing units or because the user has non-quantifiable preferences. The RFC proposes that each AR have a Policy Server that stores policy terms, synthesizes routes, and responds to host requests for policy routes. The server acts as a repository of policy knowledge for the region and can pre-compute lists of acceptable routes for administrators to prioritize. Hosts request routes from their local server with constraints (destination AR, service type, maximum cost), and the server returns the best matching route.
sections.eli5: To find a route, the system looks for a chain of rules from each network that connects your starting point to your destination. Then a person picks which chain to use based on cost, reliability, and other preferences.

sections.title: Billing and Security
sections.content: Since autonomous regions are independent, billing models vary: some charge per packet, others per byte, others use annual fees. The RFC proposes bilateral conditions in policy terms to specify collection points and billing agreements. Each AR can bill separately or delegate to another AR. To prevent fraud, policy routes should be sealed or signed by the Policy Server that created them, using cryptographic techniques. This prevents modification of the user class identifier or charge code. Detection and redress may be more effective than prevention; ARs can audit sealed routes as evidence of their origin. Security also requires managing charge codes (unique identifiers for billing) to prevent misuse and ensuring that only authorized ARs can use certain routes. An experimental migration plan proposes three phases: first, Policy Servers with temporary features to mimic gateways and hosts; second, adding policy controls to some gateways and modifying some hosts; third, full deployment. This allows experimentation without updating all infrastructure at once.
sections.eli5: Different networks charge different amounts, and they need to bill each other. Routes get signed to prove who created them and to prevent tampering. The system uses detection and accounting rather than preventing every possible fraud.
